name: Ghostbridge Island
description:
Mackinac Island banned automobiles in 1898. In 2200, it has banned everything else. The island sits in the Straits of Mackinac, 5 kilometers from the bridge that connects Michigan's two peninsulas, and it has leveraged its historical no-motor ordinance into something unprecedented in the GLMZ: a technology restriction zone. No motorized vehicles. No neural interface connectivity. No augmentation uplinks. No corporate sovereign territory. No surveillance infrastructure. The island operates under a municipal charter that predates corporate sovereignty law, and the charter's technology restrictions have been upheld by every court that's reviewed them — not because the courts agree with the principle, but because the precedent of overturning a 200-year-old municipal ordinance terrifies the legal establishment.

The result is an island of 600 permanent residents and up to 5,000 visitors at any time, living in conditions that most GLMZ inhabitants would consider medieval. Horse-drawn transport. Paper documents. Face-to-face communication. No data trail. No surveillance record. No jurisdictional tracking. The implications have not been lost on anyone. Ghostbridge Island is the GLMZ's premiere dead-drop location, negotiation venue, and disappearance destination. If you need to have a conversation that no system can record, you have it here. If you need to meet someone without creating a data point, you meet here. If you need to vanish, the island's analog infrastructure means you were never digitally here in the first place.

The Grand Hotel — a Victorian-era structure maintained in deliberately anachronistic condition — serves as the island's primary venue for the negotiations, deals, and betrayals that require total surveillance absence. The hotel's guest list is not recorded digitally. The rooms are not monitored. The staff are hired for discretion, paid in physical currency, and trained in the art of not seeing things. Ghostbridge Island is a loophole in the GLMZ's total information architecture — a place where the panopticon blinks — and every powerful interest in the Great Lakes knows it, uses it, and fears what happens when someone else uses it.

sights: Horse-drawn carriages on streets with no power lines, no signal towers, no surveillance cameras
The Grand Hotel's 200-meter porch, overlooking the Straits, populated by people whose faces you are not supposed to remember
The Mackinac Bridge visible from the east shore — the hypermodern world, close enough to see, far enough to deny
Victorian architecture maintained with deliberate precision — not nostalgia, but infrastructure for anonymity
Visitors unconsciously reaching for neural interfaces that don't connect — the phantom limb of a disconnected world
sounds: Horse hooves on pavement — the island's primary transportation sound
Human conversation without the overlay of augmented reality — raw, unfiltered, and strangely intimate
Lake water on the shoreline — the sound of a place where nature is louder than technology
The absence of electronic noise — no hums, no pings, no background data traffic — a silence most visitors have never experienced
smells: Horse, hay, and leather — the organic infrastructure of pre-motor transportation
Mackinac Island fudge — still produced, still sold, still the island's most innocent tradition
Lake Huron air, unprocessed and unfiltered — what air smelled like before the cities
atmosphere.feel: Uncanny. Ghostbridge Island feels like a glitch in the timeline — a place where 2200 forgot to arrive. The sensation of disconnection is physical for augmented visitors. Neural interfaces go silent. Uplinks drop. You are alone with your unaugmented senses, and for most GLMZ residents, that is the most disorienting experience available. It is also, for some, the most honest.

demographics: 600 permanent residents. Self-selected for analog life, multi-generational island families mixed with people who chose disconnection deliberately. Up to 5,000 transient visitors — a rotating population of fixers, negotiators, fugitives, diplomats, and tourists who want to know what silence feels like.
economy: Hospitality, dead-drop services, and the anonymity premium. The island charges for what the rest of the GLMZ cannot provide: unrecorded space. The Grand Hotel's rates are astronomical. The smaller inns and boarding houses serve the same function at lower price points. The economy is entirely analog — physical currency, paper ledgers, handshake agreements. GDP is unmeasurable by design.
power_structure: Municipal charter authority, enforced by the island's own constabulary and the legal precedent that protects the technology restriction zone. No corporate sovereign territory. No state jurisdiction beyond what the charter permits. The island's governance is the closest thing to genuine self-determination in the GLMZ, sustained not by power but by legal precedent and the useful fiction that the island is too small to matter.
dangers: The lack of surveillance means the lack of emergency response infrastructure — violence here is private and unreported
Dead-drop operations gone wrong — the island's anonymity attracts people with things to hide, and some of those things are dangerous
The legal precedent protecting the technology restriction zone is always one court challenge away from collapse
Being recognized in a place designed for anonymity — some visitors take the unrecorded status very seriously
The ferry crossing — the 5-kilometer strait is the only access, and it can be watched even if the island cannot
opportunities: Unrecorded meetings — the island's primary commodity is surveillance absence
Dead-drop facilitation — serving as intermediary for information exchanges that cannot happen on the grid
Disappearance infrastructure — the island's analog systems can absorb identities that need to stop existing
The Grand Hotel's network of contacts — the staff know everyone who matters and remember nothing officially
story_hooks: A negotiation at the Grand Hotel between two corporate sovereigns has gone wrong, and both parties are trapped on an island with no communications and no way to call for backup
The technology restriction zone's legal challenge has reached a court that might actually rule against it — and the island's permanent residents are preparing for a siege
Someone has been leaving analog messages at dead-drop sites across the island — written in a code that predates digital encryption — and the messages describe events that haven't happened yet

adjacent_to: The Mackinac Bridge (5 kilometers east — the physical link to the modern world)
Lockhaven South (Sault Ste. Marie, north via the UP shore)
The I-75 Spine (south, via the bridge to the lower peninsula)

frequented_by: Fixers, negotiators, and intermediaries who need unrecorded space
Fugitives and people in the process of becoming someone else
The 600 permanent residents who chose this life and defend it
